To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) there are positive associations among intramyocellular triglyceride, intrahepatic lipid, and visceral fat; and 2) there is an inverse association between intrahepatic fat and whole body insulin sensitivity.
1) IHTG is associated with peripheral, not hepatic, insulin resistance, and 2) IHTG may play a role in the development of peripheral insulin resistance in humans.

in nondiabetic humans, the amount of triglyceride stored in skeletal muscle (intramyocellular lipid, IMCL) and in the liver (intrahepatic triglceride, IHTG), and the amount of visceral fat (VF) are all correlated with one another.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of intrahepatic and intramyocellular triglyceride accumulation in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance.
the role that excess fat accumulation in the liver and muscle play in the development of insulin resistance.
the role of ectopic fat accumulation in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increased IHTG is associated with increased peripheral insulin resistance.
IHTG, but not IMCL, SF, or VF, is associated with peripheral and systemic insulin resistance in nondiabetic individuals.
hepatic fat accumulation is a key factor in the development of peripheral insulin resistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

increased intrahepatic fat content is associated with decreased peripheral insulin sensitivity, and that this relationship is stronger than the associations observed for intramyocellular fat or visceral fat.
increased intrahepatic and intramyocellular fat content is associated with peripheral and systemic insulin resistance.
the mass of IHTG is strongly correlated with peripheral insulin resistance, while the mass of IMCL, VF, and even abdominal SF is not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increased IHTG is associated with peripheral IR.

the mass/content (or amount) of IHTG, not IMCL, is most tightly correlated with whole body R(d), suggesting that IHTG may be the most important fat depot to target for improving whole body insulin sensitivity.
IHTG is the strongest correlate of whole body R(d), and this finding suggests that IHTG may be a useful marker of systemic insulin resistance.
